Kazumasa Yamada, Shinya Yoshikawa, Mutsuo Ichinomiya, Akira Kuwata, Mitsunobu Kamiya, Kaori Ohki. PLoS ONE View on Pubmed PUBLISHED: 01-01-2014 The order Parmales (Heterokontophyta) is a group of small-sized unicellular marine phytoplankton, which is distributed widely from tropical to polar waters. The cells of Parmales are surrounded by a distinctive cell wall, which consists of several siliceous plates fitting edge to edge. Phylogenetic and morphological analyses suggest that Parmales is one of the key organisms for elucidating the evolutionary origin of Bacillariophyceae (diatoms), the most successful heterokontophyta. The effects of silicon-limitation on growth and morphogenesis of plates were stThe effects of silicon-limitation on growth and morphogenesis of plates were studied in NIES-2565, a representative species of the Parmales. Silicon limitation significantly inhibited cellular growth, reducing the growth rate by approximately 50% compared to silicon-replete conditions. Morphologically, the siliceous cell wall plates became irregular in shape, with reduced size and disrupted patterns, suggesting a direct dependence on silicon availability for proper plate formation. These findings highlight the critical role of silicon in the biology of Parmales and underscore their evolutionary relevance to diatoms, which similarly rely on silica for cell wall biogenesis. The study emphasizes the importance of silicon cycling in marine ecosystems and provides insights into the adaptive strategies of these phytoplankton under nutrient stress. For further visualization of experimental techniques or morphological changes, the related JoVE Visualize video likely demonstrates methods such as cell culture, silicon starvation protocols, and microscopic analysis of plate structures. texts.full_text: published in print yesterday in The Times’ “Sunday Review” opinion section. The author is one Louis Hyman (a name new to me), listed as an “economic historian”—an excellent start—and director of the Institute for Workplace Studies at the ILR School at Cornell. What is “the myth of Main Street?” In Mr. Hyman’s recounting: Main Street is a place but it is also an idea. It’s small-town retail. It’s locally owned shops selling products to hardworking townspeople. It’s neighbors with dependable blue-collar jobs in auto plants and coal mines. It’s a feeling of community and of having control over your life. It’s everything, in short, that seems threatened by global capitalism and cosmopolitan elites in big cities and fancy suburbs. Mr. Hyman’s hook for his article is obviously—he says so—President Trump’s refrain of “making America great again,” which can without fear of contradiction be deeme...deemed a thinly veiled attack on the very fabric that Main Street represents: working-class Americans who have been increasingly marginalized by globalization and urbanization. Mr. Hyman argues that this nostalgia for an idealized, idyllic America is not only misguided but also rooted in a flawed understanding of history itself. He contends that "Main Street" was never actually representative of the vast majority of American experience during its heyday; rather, it represented the interests and privilege of those who owned small businesses or worked directly with their hands. texts.full_text: (2). Gas production within the necrotic tissues led to severe swelling of the affected area with bullae formation on the skin surface. The child was initially treated in a local hospital where he underwent debridement and received intravenous antibiotics. However, despite these measures, his condition deteriorated rapidly due to progressive gas accumulation causing significant tissue destruction (3). He developed systemic symptoms including fever, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, confusion, seizures, and eventually respiratory failure. The child was transferred to our institution where an emergent amputation of the affected limb from below-knee level was performed. During surgery, gas production within necrotic tissues was observed along with extensive fascial edema (4). Postoperatively, he received intensive care including mechanical ventilation due to acute respiratory distress syndrome and a combination therapy consisting of penicillin G plus clindamycin. The postoperative course revealed an improvement in his general condition. He remained on broad-spectrum antibiotics for two weeks until the wound healed completely without signs of infection or recurrence (5). The patient was discharged from hospital after four months, with good recovery and no complications at a follow-up visit three years later. This case highlights that gas gangrene can occur even in children despite its rarity. Early diagnosis is critical to prevent severe morbidity and mortality due to the rapid progression of this disease if not promptly treated (6). The occurrence also underscores the importance of parental supervision during playtime, especially when young children are exposed to potentially dangerous objects like electric saws. References: 1. texts.full_text: Turkish cystic fibrosis patients. The majority of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients suffer from chronic respiratory infection with the opportunistic bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The virulence of P. aeruginosa is associated with the presence of various extracellular factors, like alginate, elastase, alkaline protease which contribute tissue destruction and assist bacterial invasion. Virulence factor production of P. aeruginosa strains isolated from Turkish pulmonary fibrosis (fC) patients was conducted to identify their potential influence on clinical outcomes. The research aimed at typing the various isolates based on certain virulent characteristics, such as alginate expression and kinase activity levels among individuals. These factors are important in identifying how aggressive a strain can be within an infected host environment. Isolating these strains allowed scientists not only to identify them but also to identify their pathogenic potential with scientific data from patients suffering chronic Pseudomonas infections, thus shedding light on the relation between bacterial virulence and disease progression among Turkish CF population. This data is essential for implementing more targeted clinical methods targeted at controlling chronic vascular disease in pulmonary lung.
